outcome: No proof or disproof of the infinitude of primes of the form n²+1 has been posted or accepted since 26 January 2024; the window holds partial bounds on the largest prime factor of n²+1 (Pascadi 2024; Harman 2024; Li 2024–2025; Cuevas–Pasten 2025; Grimmelt–Merikoski 2025; Pasten 1 September 2026, whose Corollary 1.2 its author credits to the AI model ChatGPT-5.6 Sol Pro), a shifted-primes square-divisor result (Li 2025), and unrefereed claimed proofs of Bunyakovsky/Bateman–Horn-type statements that cover n²+1 by generality (Aabidi El Moussati, May 2025; Xiao, December 2025, not opened); the Wikipedia article (last edited 3 June 2026) and an AIM problem list (May 2026) still describe the problem as open.
problem_asks: Are there infinitely many primes of the form n²+1? Unpacked: for n ranging over the positive integers, the set of primes p with p = n²+1 for some n is infinite (equivalently, n²+1 is prime for infinitely many n). The bullet is a single existence question. It asks for no bound, no density or asymptotic, no restriction on n, and no Gaussian-prime, almost-prime, or largest-prime-factor version. The parent (Landau's problems) lists four problems; this bullet is the first of them, and its statement stands alone.

events.what_happened: Mahler (1933) and Chowla (1934) gave the classical lower bound that the largest prime factor P(n²+1) grows at least like log₂ n (iterated logarithm). This is recounted in Pasten's 2026 preprint (arXiv 2609.01327) and in the abstract of his 2023 preprint ('going back to work of Chowla in 1934'). The original papers were not opened; the dating comes from the 2026 text as returned by a summarising fetch.
events.delivers: A lower bound P(n²+1) ≥ c·log₂ n for large n. It concerns the largest prime factor only and says nothing about whether n²+1 is prime.
events.time_since_posted: about 93 years; cited as background by the 2023 and 2026 Pasten preprints and by Quanta (October 2024), with no separate verification sought
events.direction: Lower bound on the largest prime factor; does not bear on whether n²+1 is prime infinitely often.

events.what_happened: Henryk Iwaniec, 'Almost-primes represented by quadratic polynomials' (Inventiones Mathematicae 47 (1978), pp. 171–188, from search results; the journal page was not opened). He proved that n²+1 has at most two prime factors (counted with multiplicity) for infinitely many n. Vishaal Kapoor's exposition (arXiv 1910.02885, submitted 26 September 2019) quotes this and follows Iwaniec's proof, which uses a Richert weighted sum and a linear sieve.
events.delivers: Infinitely many n for which n²+1 is a product of at most two primes (almost-primes). It does not give prime values; this is a different question from the bullet.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The almost-prime result is the closest classical approach and does not answer whether n²+1 is prime.

checked_by.qualification: Masters-level essay (2006 M.Sc.), not an expert referee
checked_by.what_they_did: Worked through Iwaniec's proof and extended it to irreducible quadratic polynomials G(n)

events.direction: Partial result toward the problem (almost-primes), not toward prime values. It leaves the bullet's question open.

events.what_happened: Chengyan Liu, 'Sieve Method and Landau Problem' (arXiv math/9909154, math.GM, one version, submitted 25 September 1999). The abstract says 'We solve Landau's four unattackable problems, including Goldbach Conjecture and Twin Prime Conjecture through sieve method.' The page does not mention n²+1 by name and contains no argument.
events.revisions: v1 25 Sep 1999 only.
events.delivers: Claimed (abstract only) to solve all four Landau problems, which includes the n²+1 problem by implication. No proof is on the page, so the scope of what is actually shown cannot be read.
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim held. The page gives no argument to check, and the other three problems are still listed as open by Wikipedia (fetched June 2026).
events.doubts: A one-line abstract claims to solve all four Landau problems, including Goldbach and the twin prime conjecture, which the 2026 Wikipedia article still lists as unresolved (fetched). No argument is on the page. Basis: the arXiv abstract page read and the Wikipedia status line.
events.direction: Claims a proof of the infinitude statement by implication, so it cuts toward the conjectured answer (infinitely many).

events.what_happened: Stewart and Yu (2001) developed a transcendence-theory method for lower bounds on the largest prime factor of polynomial values; Haristoy (2003) applied it to n²+1 for a small improvement. Both are described in Quanta's October 2024 article, which was opened. The original papers were not opened.
events.delivers: Small improvements to the lower bound on P(n²+1). Quantities are about the largest prime factor and not prime values.
events.time_since_posted: about 23 years for the first of these
events.direction: Bound on the largest prime factor only; does not bear on the bullet's question.

events.what_happened: Sławomir Kurpaska and Apoloniusz Tyszka, arXiv 1506.08655 (first submitted June 2015; many later versions, search results show up to v34). Per search-snippet summaries (not opened), the paper takes the infinitude of primes n²+1 (Landau's conjecture) as the premise of a heuristic statement Φ with an explicit bound and poses an open problem about a set X ⊆ N, which they argue cannot be formalised in ZFC.
events.revisions: v1 June 2015; revised through at least 2023 under different titles (search-snippet level).
events.delivers: Nothing on the bullet's question. The statement Φ is heuristic (the authors say so, per the snippet), and the paper is about a set-theoretic status claim.
events.direction: Does not cut either way on the bullet; it uses the conjecture as a premise.

events.what_happened: Jori Merikoski, 'On the largest prime factor of n²+1' (arXiv 1908.08816, first posted 23 August 2019; v2 27 August 2019; v3 2 November 2020). Unconditionally, P(n²+1) > n^1.279 for infinitely many n, improving de la Bretèche–Drappeau's 1.2182 via a new Type II estimate and Harman's sieve. Conditionally on Selberg's eigenvalue conjecture, the exponent may be raised to 1.312. Journal: J. Eur. Math. Soc. 25(4) (2023), pp. 1253–1284; submitted 5 December 2019, accepted 26 October 2020, published online 5 February 2022 (EMS page).
events.revisions: arXiv v1 23 Aug 2019; v2 27 Aug 2019; v3 2 Nov 2020; JEMS accepted 26 Oct 2020, published online 5 Feb 2022.
events.delivers: Unconditional: P(n²+1) > n^1.279 for infinitely many n. Conditional on Selberg's eigenvalue conjecture: exponent 1.312. Both are bounds on the largest prime factor and neither produces prime values.

checked_by.who: Journal of the European Mathematical Society (refereed)
checked_by.what_they_did: Refereed and accepted the paper (accepted 26 October 2020)

checked_by.who: University of Turku doctoral committee (reviewers Roger Baker and Kevin Ford; opponent James Maynard; supervisor Kaisa Matomäki)
checked_by.what_they_did: Approved the 2021 thesis Approximations to Landau's problems on prime numbers, whose fourth article is on the largest prime factor of n²+1 (search-snippet level)

events.direction: Lower bound on the largest prime factor, unconditional at 1.279. It does not bear on the prime-value question directly.

events.what_happened: Frank Vega, 'Near-Square Primes Conjecture' (EasyChair Preprint 4119; Zenodo copies). The abstract says 'This problem remains open' and then 'We prove this conjecture is indeed true.' The argument, as excerpted in search results (the full PDF was not read), uses Wilson's theorem: assume finitely many such primes, so that n²+1 is eventually composite, then derive that (n²)!/(n²+1) is eventually an integer, and contradict a lemma on irrational multiples. Six EasyChair versions: 1 Sep 2020 (v1, v2 'fixed some details'), 8 Sep ('updated Definition 1.1'), 14 Sep ('minor changes: abstract and content'), 7 Oct ('shorter proof'), 23 Nov 2020 (v6, 'content changes'). The Zenodo copy (record 4011301) lists creator Frank Vega, affiliation CopSonic.
events.revisions: EasyChair v1 and v2 1 Sep 2020; v3 8 Sep 2020; v4 14 Sep 2020; v5 7 Oct 2020; v6 23 Nov 2020. Zenodo record 4011301 lists version 6 with publication date 1 Sep 2020; the Zenodo dates were not reconciled with EasyChair.
events.delivers: Claimed: infinitely many primes of the form n²+1 (the full bullet). The argument as excerpted is not shown to establish the non-integrality step it needs (see doubts).
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim held. The reviewable step is missing from what was read.
events.doubts: (1) Wilson's theorem: for m = n²+1 > 4, m divides (m−1)! unless m is prime, in which case (m−1)! ≡ −1 (mod m). So '(n²)!/(n²+1) is an integer for all large n' holds exactly when n²+1 is composite for all large n, which is the negation of the conjecture. The contradiction therefore needs an independent lemma that the ratio is non-integral for infinitely many n; the excerpted argument invokes a lemma about irrational multiples, while the ratio is rational. This is my own check from the excerpted description, not a published review. (2) Six versions between 1 September and 23 November 2020 changed the definitions and shortened the proof, and no version was refereed or endorsed. (3) The problem is still listed as open by the AIM problem list (May 2026, search-snippet level) and the Wikipedia article (fetched June 2026), and neither cites the preprint.
events.direction: Claims the conjecture is true, so it cuts toward the conjectured answer (infinitely many).

events.what_happened: Yeisson Alexis Acevedo Agudelo, 'Prime numbers. An alternative study using ova-angular rotations' (arXiv 2104.04522, math.GM, submitted 11 April 2021; v2 2 September 2021; JP Journal of Algebra, Number Theory and Applications, 2021). The abstract lists among its applications 'the existence of infinite primes of the form ρ = k²+1'. The abstract does not call this a proof, and the body was not available in the fetched text.
events.revisions: v1 11 Apr 2021; v2 2 Sep 2021 (current).
events.delivers: Claimed (abstract only) that there are infinitely many primes of the form k²+1 as an application of an elementary geometric theory. The argument is not visible.
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim held. The argument is not read.

checked_by.who: JP Journal of Algebra, Number Theory and Applications
checked_by.qualification: Journal reference only; refereeing procedure not verified
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (journal reference from arXiv page)

events.doubts: A single-author paper whose n²+1 claim appears only as one item in an abstract that says the mathematics is elementary; the abstract is the only text read and it gives no argument. The claim is contrary to the open status recorded by Wikipedia (June 2026), which does not cite it. Basis: the arXiv abstract page and the Wikipedia status line.
events.direction: Claims infinitude, so it cuts toward the conjectured answer.

events.what_happened: N. A. Carella, 'Largest Prime Factors of Polynomials' (arXiv 2308.10075, math.GM, first posted 19 August 2023; revisions to v7 on 13 June 2025). The abstract shows that the largest prime factor p of the product of n²+1 over x ≤ n ≤ 2x satisfies p ≥ x^{3/2} for large x, improving the earlier x^{1.279} estimate. The version that first carried the x^{3/2} bound was not identified.
events.delivers: A lower bound on the largest prime factor of a product of n²+1 over an interval. It is about a product over many n rather than a single value and says nothing about whether any n²+1 is prime.
events.direction: Bound on the largest prime factor of an interval product; a different question from the bullet.

events.what_happened: Valerii Sopin, 'Existence of a Quadratic Polynomial, Which Represents Infinitely Many Prime Numbers: Bunyakovsky's Conjecture for Degree Greater than One and the 4th Landau Problem' (EasyChair Preprint 8203; the fetched page is tz6v). The abstract says 'No single case of Bunyakovsky's conjecture for degree greater than one has been proved' and claims to overcome this using the Friedlander–Iwaniec theorem, sums of two squares, the Brahmagupta–Fibonacci identity and Bézout's lemma. Versions: v1 7 June 2022 (no note); v2 15 November 2023 (note: 'there exist infinitely many integers n such that n²+1 is either prime or the product of two primes'); v3 18 November 2023 (extended Euclidean algorithm); v4 20 November 2023 (Hyperbolic Prime Number Theorem). The date given is v3, the first version whose abstract makes the degree-two claim as fetched.
events.delivers: Claimed: a quadratic polynomial represents infinitely many primes. Per a search-level summary of the PDF, the statement is reformulated as: for some integer c, f(N)+c contains infinitely many primes. That is not the classical statement f(N) prime infinitely often, and the page does not name n²+1 as the polynomial.
events.remains: If the reformulation is what is proved, the classical question for n²+1 (with c = 0) remains open. The page does not decide that.
events.doubts: The statement proved appears to be a reformulation with an integer shift c, which is weaker than the classical statement (per the search-level summary of the PDF, not read in full). The v2 note also states a weaker almost-prime claim, so the claim changes across versions. No journal, referee or expert response was found.
events.direction: Claims infinitude for some quadratic polynomial, under a reformulation; cuts toward the conjectured answer only if read in the classical form.

events.what_happened: Hector Pasten, 'The largest prime factor of n²+1 and improvements on subexponential ABC' (arXiv 2312.03566, one version, 6 December 2023). Combining transcendental methods with modular approaches to the abc conjecture, it shows that P(n²+1) ≥ (log₂ n)²/log₃ n for large n, with log_k the k-th iterate of the logarithm. Press reports (Chilean university and Meganoticias, April 2024; not opened) say the paper was published in Inventiones Mathematicae; the journal page was not opened.
events.revisions: v1 6 Dec 2023 only.
events.delivers: A lower bound on the largest prime factor of n²+1 for large n. It is not a statement about prime values.

checked_by.who: Inventiones Mathematicae (per press coverage only; not verified at the journal)
checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal of record, if the press report is right
checked_by.what_they_did: Reportedly accepted and published the paper

checked_by.qualification: Expert science journalist; a digest, not a verification
checked_by.what_they_did: Explained the 2024 result in lay terms, quoting the bound as (log log n)², which matches the iterated-log form

events.direction: Lower bound on the largest prime factor; does not bear on prime values.

events.what_happened: Glyn Harman, 'Two problems on the greatest prime factor of n²+1' (Acta Arithmetica 213 (2024), pp. 273–287; published online 21 February 2024; no preprint was checked). The note reduces an exponent in the count of n ≤ x with P⁺(n²+1) below x^α (α > 4/5) to 0.567 using the de la Bretèche–Drappeau method and Kim's eigenvalue bound, and uses Merikoski's large-value work to improve the Everest–Harman results on primitive divisors of n²+1.
events.revisions: Published online 21 Feb 2024; no earlier arXiv version checked.
events.delivers: Results on the distribution of P⁺(n²+1) and on primitive divisors. These are about the size of the largest prime factor, not about primality.
events.direction: Size-of-prime-factor results only; does not bear on the bullet's question.

events.what_happened: Alexandru Pascadi, 'Large sieve inequalities for exceptional Maass forms and the greatest prime factor of n²+1' (arXiv 2404.04239, first posted 5 April 2024). It proves new large sieve inequalities for exceptional Maass forms and, as an application, that the greatest prime factor of n²+1 is infinitely often greater than n^1.3, improving Merikoski's n^1.279. The abstract says 'we show', with no hypothesis named.
events.revisions: v1 5 Apr 2024; v2 8 Jan 2025 ('small improvements & removed two applications'); v3 15 Jan 2026 ('Incorporates referees' comments (to appear in Forum Math. Pi)').
events.delivers: Unconditional (as stated, the page does not use the word): P(n²+1) > n^1.3 for infinitely many n. A bound on the largest prime factor only.

checked_by.who: Referees of Forum of Mathematics, Pi (anonymous)
checked_by.what_they_did: Refereed the paper; the author's v3 note says it incorporates the referees' comments and is 'to appear in Forum Math. Pi'. Acceptance not confirmed on the journal page.

events.direction: Bound on the largest prime factor; does not bear on prime values.

events.what_happened: Runbo Li, arXiv 2406.07575, version 1 (6 June 2024), titled 'On the primitive divisors of quadratic polynomials'. It gives a new upper bound for the number of integers n ≤ x for which n²+1 has a primitive divisor, improving a result of Harman and building on Pascadi's work on the largest prime factor of n²+1 (abstract read; the explicit constant was not found).
events.revisions: v1 6 Jun 2024 (titled 'On the primitive divisors of quadratic polynomials'); v2 31 May 2025 (retitled 'On the largest prime factor of quadratic polynomials'; see the 2025 event).
events.delivers: An upper bound on how many n ≤ x have n²+1 with a primitive divisor. This is a counting result about a property of n²+1, not about its primality.
events.direction: Counting result on primitive divisors; does not bear on the bullet's question.

events.what_happened: Ben Green and Mehtaab Sawhney, 'Primes of the form p² + nq²' (arXiv 2410.04189, first posted 5 October 2024; v2 12 October 2024; v3 6 June 2026 corrects a partial summation error in Section 8.3 and a minor inaccuracy in 8.7). For n ≡ 0 or 4 mod 6 they show there are infinitely many primes p² + nq² with p and q both prime, with an asymptotic. For n = 4 this verifies the Gaussian primes conjecture of Friedlander and Iwaniec (p² + 4q²). This is a different family: the prime is a sum of two squares-type form, not n²+1. The abstract was read.
events.revisions: v1 5 Oct 2024; v2 12 Oct 2024; v3 6 Jun 2026 (corrections in Sections 8.3 and 8.7).
events.delivers: Infinitely many primes of the form p² + nq² with p and q prime, for n ≡ 0 or 4 mod 6. This is a different family from n²+1, and no n²+1 instance is established.
events.direction: A neighbouring theorem on a different polynomial family; it neither settles nor moves the bullet's question.

events.what_happened: Jon Grantham and Hester Graves, 'Primes of the Form m²+1 and Goldbach's Other Other Conjecture' (arXiv 2502.03513, posted 5 February 2025, one version). They compute all primes of the form m²+1 up to 6.25 × 10^28 and test a Goldbach variant up to that bound. They introduce 'Goldbach champions' and prove conditional results about them, assuming either Schinzel's Hypothesis H or the Bateman–Horn conjecture.
events.revisions: v1 5 Feb 2025 only.
events.delivers: A finite census of primes m²+1 up to 6.25 × 10^28 (unconditional computation), and conditional results on Goldbach champions. A finite census of instances of an infinitude claim moves nothing; the conditional results are not about the unconditional question.
events.directly_checkable: The finite list of primes m²+1 up to 6.25 × 10^28 can be rechecked value by value with a primality test; the abstract does not describe the verification method beyond 'calculations'.
events.direction: Finite census; neither cuts for nor against the infinitude statement.

events.what_happened: José Cuevas Barrientos and Hector Pasten, 'On the greatest prime factor of polynomial values and subexponential Szpiro in families' (arXiv 2504.15971, first posted 22 April 2025). The abstract combines Pasten's modular approach to abc with linear forms in logarithms and gives unconditional bounds for Szpiro's conjecture in families and for the greatest prime factor of quadratic and cubic polynomial values. It says the polynomial bound 'extends earlier work by the second author for the polynomial n²+1'. The theorems were not read.
events.revisions: v1 22 Apr 2025; v2 4 Aug 2025; v3 7 Sep 2025 ('Fixed some references').
events.delivers: Unconditional lower bounds for the greatest prime factor of quadratic and cubic polynomial values. For n²+1 the page only says the bound extends Pasten's earlier result, without giving it. Bounds on the largest prime factor do not produce prime values.
events.direction: Bound on the largest prime factor of polynomial values; does not bear on the bullet's question.

events.what_happened: Lasse Grimmelt and Jori Merikoski, 'On the greatest prime factor and uniform equidistribution of quadratic polynomials' (arXiv 2505.00493, first posted 1 May 2025; v2 30 May 2025 'minor corrections'). The abstract says they show that the greatest prime factor of n²+h is at least n^1.312 for infinitely many n, an unconditional proof for a range previously known under the Selberg eigenvalue conjecture (h = 1 is n²+1). Uniformity in h ≤ n^(1+o(1)) depends on a hypothesis on real characters. The method uses SL₂(ℝ) spectral methods, avoiding Kloosterman sums. Grimmelt gave a Bristol seminar talk on 4 March 2026 (search-level).
events.revisions: v1 1 May 2025; v2 30 May 2025 ('minor corrections').
events.delivers: For h = 1, P(n²+1) ≥ n^1.312 for infinitely many n, unconditional. The uniform-in-h statements are conditional. These are bounds on the largest prime factor and do not produce prime values.
events.doubts: Runbo Li's v2 (31 May 2025) reports exponent 1.317 for n²+1 from this result, while the Grimmelt–Merikoski abstract states 1.312. The gap is not explained in the text read (see disputes). No journal version was found.
events.direction: Bound on the largest prime factor; does not bear on prime values.

events.what_happened: Runbo Li, 'Largest square divisors of shifted primes' (arXiv 2505.23779, first posted 16 May 2025; v2 17 October 2025). The abstract shows there are infinitely many primes p such that, for any nonzero integer a, p − a is divisible by a square d² > p^(1/2 + 1/700), improving Merikoski's 1/2 + 1/2000. The thesis (Turku 2021) presents this line as an approximation to the n²+1 conjecture, because p − 1 = n² when p = n²+1.
events.delivers: A square-divisor bound for infinitely many shifted primes p − a, uniform in a. It does not require p to be of the form n²+1, and it does not show that any p − 1 is a square.
events.direction: A related approximation (square divisors of shifted primes), not a result about n²+1 itself.

events.what_happened: Abdeslam Aabidi El Moussati, 'Symbolic Resolution of the Bunyakovsky Conjecture via AION' (Cambridge Open Engage working paper, posted 29 May 2025; the page says it has not been peer-reviewed). The abstract claims that polynomials with integer coefficients that are irreducible, have a positive leading term and lack a fixed divisor escape all symbolic multiplicative constructions infinitely often, and that this 'confirms the infinite occurrence of prime outputs'. It says the argument 'requires no probabilistic or analytic tools'. Similar titles on the same platform (Goldbach, Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer, Beal, Riemann; search-snippet level, not opened) use the same AION framing.
events.revisions: Version 1 only (per the Cambridge Engage page).
events.delivers: Claimed: infinitely many prime values for the whole Bunyakovsky class described. n²+1 is in that class (irreducible, positive leading term, no fixed divisor), so the claim would settle the bullet if correct. The page does not mention n²+1 and gives no proof steps.
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim held. The argument is not shown on the page.
events.doubts: The abstract gives no argument, and the framework ('AION irreducibility model') is not defined on the page, so the claim cannot be checked from it. The page itself states the work has not been peer-reviewed. The claim is for the full Bunyakovsky class, which the Jones–Zvonkin 2021 survey (search-snippet level) and the Encyclopedia of Mathematics entry (search-snippet level) describe as proved only for degree 1, so the claim goes beyond what the field records as known. Basis: the Cambridge Engage page read directly and the snippet-level summaries of the other sources.
events.direction: Claims infinitely many prime values for the whole class that contains n²+1; cuts toward the conjectured answer.

events.what_happened: Runbo Li, 'On the largest prime factor of quadratic polynomials' (arXiv 2406.07575, version 2, 31 May 2025). The abstract states that a result of Grimmelt and Merikoski implies that the largest prime factor of n²+1 exceeds x^1.317 infinitely often, and applies this to the number of n ≤ x for which n²+1 has a primitive divisor. The paper does not state whether the result is unconditional.
events.revisions: v1 6 Jun 2024 ('On the primitive divisors of quadratic polynomials'); v2 31 May 2025 (retitled; the 1.317 claim first appears here).
events.delivers: Claims P(n²+1) > x^1.317 for infinitely many x (a bound on the largest prime factor). The cited Grimmelt–Merikoski abstract states 1.312 for this case. The derivation of 1.317 from that result is not shown in the text read.
events.doubts: The exponent 1.317 disagrees with the 1.312 stated in the source it cites (arXiv 2505.00493), and the difference is not explained in the abstract read. The unconditional status of the 1.317 claim is not stated.
events.direction: Bound on the largest prime factor; does not bear on prime values.

events.what_happened: Huan Xiao, 'From Golomb to Bateman–Horn' (Preprints.org, DOI 10.20944/preprints202512.2666.v1, posted 31 December 2025; labelled 'Not peer-reviewed version'). Per a search snippet, the abstract says the Bateman–Horn conjecture is a conjecture on prime values in polynomials and 'We prove it by Golomb's method'. The author's affiliation is given as the School of Artificial Intelligence, Zhuhai City Polytechnic. The page returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch, so the full text and any AI statement were NOT checked.
events.revisions: v1 31 Dec 2025 (the only version seen). Companion preprints by the same author, per search snippets, are 'From Golomb to Schinzel' (June 2025) and 'From Bateman-Horn to Chowla' (January 2026); not checked.
events.delivers: Claimed: the Bateman–Horn conjecture in full. For f(n) = n²+1 (irreducible, no fixed divisor), Bateman–Horn predicts and would give infinitely many n with n²+1 prime, so the claim would settle the bullet if it held. The scope of the claim was not confirmed.
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim held. The full text was not read.
events.doubts: Per a search snippet of a Hindry–Rivoal survey (not opened), Golomb's method rests on a single analytic step (interchanging a limit and a series) that the method does not supply, and Conrad adapted the method to Bateman–Horn. Whether the new preprint justifies that step was not checked, because the full text was not reachable. No response from experts, and no journal submission, was found.
events.direction: Claims the full conjecture, so it cuts toward the conjectured answer.

events.what_happened: Hector Pasten, 'An improvement on the largest prime factor of n²+1' (arXiv 2609.01327, math.NT, single author, first posted 1 September 2026). Corollary 1.2 gives a lower bound (log₂ n)²/log₄ n for the largest prime factor P(n²+1) for large n, improving the 2023 bound with log₃ n. Theorem 1.1 is an inequality (log₂ n)² bounded by a constant times log(R_n)·log₂(P_n), with R_n the radical of n²+1. The abstract adds that when the bound is nearly sharp it also holds for many prime factors of n²+1. The acknowledgements state that Corollary 1.2 and its initial proof were first obtained by an AI model (see ai). The introduction says 'The use of AI is described in the Acknowledgements section.' The introduction says the proof of Theorem 1.1 follows 'the ideas from [7]', a prior paper by the same author (summarised fetch).
events.revisions: v1 only (1 Sep 2026, 6 KB, per the arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: A lower bound on the largest prime factor of n²+1 for all large n, in the form (log₂ n)²/log₄ n (as paraphrased by the fetch tool; the constant was not read). It concerns the largest prime factor only. It produces no n with n²+1 prime and is consistent with finitely many such primes.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. Nothing in the parts of the paper that were read addresses primality of n²+1.
events.direction: A lower bound on a quantity the bullet does not name (the largest prime factor). It neither supports nor opposes the infinitude of primes n²+1.

systems.name: ChatGPT-5.6 Sol Pro
systems.what_it_did: Per the acknowledgements, first obtained Corollary 1.2 and its initial proof in an autonomous way from a single prompt in July 2026. Theorem 1.1 was 'subsequently discovered by the author from interactions with the same AI model'. The paper states 'The proof presented here is due to the author' and 'The author takes full responsibility for the content of the paper.'
systems.basis_quote: Corollary 1.2 and its initial proof were first obtained in an autonomous way by the AI model ChatGPT-5.6 Sol Pro after a single prompt in July 2026.

disputes.summary: For n²+1, Runbo Li's v2 abstract (31 May 2025) gives the exponent 1.317 and attributes it to Grimmelt and Merikoski; the Grimmelt–Merikoski abstract (1 May 2025) states 1.312 for n²+h. The difference is not explained in the text read.

Pasten's 2026 preprint credits ChatGPT-5.6 Sol Pro with first obtaining Corollary 1.2 and its initial proof, and says the proof presented is the author's. The attribution is the author's own statement; no competing claim was found.

A search-level listing for Vega's 2020 preprint gave a different creator in one Zenodo copy. The Zenodo record read (4011301) lists Frank Vega, with affiliation CopSonic, so the creator is taken as Vega.

summary: Nothing since 26 January 2024 settles whether there are infinitely many primes of the form n²+1, and no proof or disproof has been refereed. The in-window output is of two kinds. First, bounds on the largest prime factor of n²+1 that do not address primality: Pascadi (5 April 2024, n^1.3 i.o.; accepted to appear in Forum Math. Pi per the author's v3 note), Harman (Acta Arithmetica, online 21 February 2024; size and primitive-divisor results), Cuevas–Pasten (22 April 2025; lower bounds for quadratic and cubic polynomials), Grimmelt–Merikoski (1 May 2025; n^1.312 i.o. for n²+h, unconditional), Li (31 May 2025; claims 1.317, which conflicts with the 1.312 of the source it cites), Carella (product over intervals, revised to June 2025), and Pasten (arXiv 2609.01327, 1 September 2026; (log₂ n)²/log₄ n). Second, unrefereed claimed proofs of statements that include n²+1 by generality: Aabidi El Moussati (Cambridge Open Engage, 29 May 2025, Bunyakovsky class via 'AION'; no argument shown on the page) and Huan Xiao (Preprints.org, 31 December 2025, Bateman–Horn via Golomb's method; full text not reachable, HTTP 403). Older claimed direct proofs: Vega (EasyChair, from 1 September 2020; circularity by Wilson's theorem, which is my own check of the excerpted argument), Acevedo Agudelo (2021, abstract only), Liu (1999, abstract only), and Sopin (2023, a reformulated statement with an integer shift). None of these claimed proofs has any public verification that I could find. Wikipedia's article (last edited 3 June 2026, fetched) still lists all four Landau problems as unresolved and cites Green–Sawhney and Grimmelt–Merikoski without mentioning any AI result or any Pasten result; the AIM 'AI and number theory' workshop problem list (May 2026, search-snippet level, the PDF not readable) lists the problem as open. The only AI attribution found for this problem is Pasten's acknowledgement (ChatGPT-5.6 Sol Pro, Corollary 1.2 and its initial proof, July 2026); Claude Opus 5 is named as used for proofreading an earlier draft, which by §5.4 is not load-bearing and is recorded here rather than in ai.systems. The quoted acknowledgement came from two summarising fetches of the arXiv HTML page, which agreed on the sentence; the PDF text did not extract, so the wording should be checked against the source before it is relied on. The system string is recorded as the paper gives it. Press and aggregator reports that name GPT-5.6 Sol, Sol Pro or Sol Ultra for other problems are not used. Whether Pasten's result counts as progress on this bullet is a close call. Corollary 1.2 is a lower bound on a quantity the bullet does not name, and it cannot produce a prime value of n²+1; on the scope test in §2.1 I read it as not moving the bullet's quantity. But the AI-credited result is the most prominent in-window event, so the event, its quotation and all its restrictions are recorded in full for the judging pass. The search for AI involvement in this problem found nothing else on n²+1: the AI-related items that did come up (OpenAI's Astra report of August 2026, GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra on the cycle double cover conjecture, Erdős problem 1141, Axiom's prime-gap formalisation, and a GPT prime-gap preprint) concern other problems. Two identical-looking names deserve care: the Erdős #1141 entry and the Lean formalisation arXiv 2608.08643 are about other conjectures, and the Lean formalisation is of the 'set of primes is supernatural' conjecture, not of this one.
competing_reading: For the AI-credited result (Pasten 2026): a judge who treats a sharper lower bound on P(n²+1) as progress on Landau's fourth problem would record this as in-window progress with AI involvement in the central corollary, since the title is 'an improvement on the largest prime factor of n²+1' and the bullet is about n²+1. For the claimed proofs (Vega 2020, Aabidi El Moussati 2025, Xiao 2025): a reader could take the authors' claims at face value and count them as resolutions, with the open status left to verification. The record does not decide either. For Vega, the excerpted argument reads as circular by Wilson's theorem, but that reading is mine and not a published review. For Xiao, the full text was not reached, so the claim is unassessed.
what_would_settle_it: For the AI-credited result: a read of the full PDF to confirm the Corollary 1.2 statement and the acknowledgement wording verbatim, plus expert checking of Corollary 1.2 and Theorem 1.1, and a statement from the judging pass on whether the largest prime factor counts as the quantity the bullet names. For the Grimmelt–Merikoski/Li discrepancy: the published version of arXiv 2505.00493 and a derivation of 1.317 from it, or a correction. For Vega: a referee report or a corrected version that proves the non-integrality of (n²)!/(n²+1) for infinitely many n by a route that does not assume the conjecture. For Aabidi El Moussati and Xiao: a full proof text and an expert reading of the step that yields infinitude. For Sopin: the exact statement proved, and whether it is the classical f(N) statement for n²+1. For Acevedo Agudelo and Liu: the body of the argument.

dead_ends: No 2026 proof or disproof of the infinitude of n^2+1 primes found in any search; no AI system credited with the problem's main question found.
Erdős problem 1141: an internal OpenAI model result on n - a k^2 primality, not n^2+1 (opened).
Lean formalisation arXiv 2608.08643 (Mayeux): formalises the statement of the 'set of primes is supernatural' conjecture; not n^2+1 (opened).
AIM Lean file (search-level): states the n^2+1 problem as a theorem with sorry; contains no proof (the statement is the only content).

OpenAI Astra (August 2026): reported ten results in other fields (sphere packing, codes, groups, Connes, Ramsey, complexity); no number-theory n^2+1 result in coverage read (secondary coverage, snippet level).
GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra, cycle double cover conjecture (July 2026), Axiom 246 prime gaps formalisation, and a GPT prime-gap 186 preprint: unrelated to n^2+1.
Matomäki's result on primes p = aq²+1 with a ≤ p^(1/2+ε) (search snippet): a different family, not opened.
Harman–Lewis on primes p = m²+n² with n ≤ p^0.119 (search snippet): a different family (sums of two squares), not opened.

Averaged Bateman–Horn results: Kravitz–Woo–Xu (Dec 2025, random polynomials), Bortolussi (2026), Volfson (June 2026), Skorobogatov–Sofos (average case); search snippets only. These are averages over families, not single-polynomial results, so they do not address n^2+1; not opened, so incomplete.
Xiao's companion preprints ('From Golomb to Schinzel', June 2025; 'From Bateman-Horn to Chowla', January 2026): search snippet only; not checked.
Pasten's 2025 coauthored note with Cuevas Barrientos: opened (see event); the theorem statements were not read.

Jones–Zvonkin (arXiv 2105.03915): used for the statement that Bunyakovsky is known only in degree 1; snippet only, not opened. The 2026 AIM list snippet and the Wikipedia fetch both list the problem as open.
Ova-angular theory follow-ups and an unrelated 'Temporal dynamics framework' item from a search: not opened and not about n^2+1 specifically.
Chilean and Spanish-language press on Pasten (2024 and 2026): snippet only; used only to date the Inventiones report and to corroborate the authorship.

incomplete: (1) The AI attribution in pasten-2026-09 rests on two summarising fetches of the arXiv HTML page, which agree on the acknowledgement sentence, but the PDF text did not extract and the quote should be checked against the source. (2) Huan Xiao's preprint (xiao-2025-12-bateman-horn) returned HTTP 403 on both the preprints.org page and the DOI redirect; its abstract comes from a search snippet and its AI involvement was not checked, so its ai.none_found true is not established. (3) The AIM 'AI and number theory' problem list (May 2026) is a PDF that did not extract; the entry for this problem is taken from a search snippet. (4) For most in-window and older events only the arXiv or journal abstract pages were read, not the full texts, so the absence of AI sentences is established only for the abstract and metadata pages read, not for acknowledgements in the full papers (e.g. Pascadi, Grimmelt–Merikoski, Li, Cuevas–Pasten, Harman, Merikoski, Pasten 2023, Carella, Acevedo Agudelo). (5) Journal publication for Pasten 2023 (Inventiones Mathematicae) and Pascadi (Forum Math. Pi) rests on press reports and an author's note; the journal pages were not opened. (6) Iwaniec (1978) and Mahler/Chowla (1933/1934) originals were not opened; their dates and results come from secondary sources. Stewart–Yu (2001) and Haristoy (2003) come from Quanta. (7) Vega's (2020) full PDF was not read; the argument and the circularity point are from search excerpts, and the circularity check is my own from Wilson's theorem, not a published review. (8) Sopin's (2023) statement and its version 1 content were not read in full; the reformulation comes from a search-level summary. (9) Aabidi El Moussati's (2025) paper gives no proof steps on its page; the AION framework is not defined there, and the companion AION titles were seen only as search results. (10) The first-posting date of Harman's (2024) note is the journal's online date; any earlier preprint was not checked. (11) The 1.317 (Li) versus 1.312 (Grimmelt–Merikoski) discrepancy is recorded and not resolved. (12) The 1.312 result for h = 1 was not checked against the full text of Grimmelt–Merikoski; only the abstract was read. (13) Averaged Bateman–Horn papers (Kravitz–Woo–Xu, Bortolussi, Volfson) and Matomäki and Harman–Lewis results were not opened; they are not about the single polynomial n^2+1 and are recorded only as dead ends. (14) The Wikipedia article was read through a summarising fetch (twice); the statement 'as of 2026, all four problems are unresolved' and the absence of any mention of the 2026 Pasten result are from that summary.
